Evaluator instruction context.

# Targeted prompt and contract editing

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Use this mode for requests such as “change how the model expresses uncertainty”
or “update this prompt and its JSON/replay contract.” Review-only requests remain
read-only. A prompt edit does not select a new development lifecycle, authorize
model calls, or invent an extraction, replay, or evaluation pipeline.

Identify the behavioral delta and actual upstream/downstream surfaces: generation
instructions, schemas/wire examples, validation, replay and versioning. Do not
invent missing extraction or evaluation layers.

## Map ownership before editing

Record the actual files, owners, inputs and consumers for each affected row. Mark
an absent surface not applicable; a missing required contract blocks that part of
the edit rather than justifying a substitute. Keep unaffected surfaces unchanged.

| Surface | Owns / coordinated change | Does not own |
|---|---|---|
| Generation instructions | Desired reasoning/output behavior, uncertainty, source restrictions and exclusions; change the behavioral rule. | Canonical identities, source timestamps, validation success or invented evidence. |
| Model-returned wire hints/examples | Exact model-returned keys, types, enums, null rules and concrete examples; synchronize with the changed rule. | Application-enriched fields or the final persisted shape masquerading as model output. |
| Strict accepted-output validation | Allowed keys/types/values, required fields, source-reference validity, quote rules and cross-field invariants; exercise examples at the real boundary. | Treating valid JSON as accepted output or downgrading rejection to compatibility fallback. |
| Application enrichment and final validation | Resolve supplied identities, verify/reconcile evidence and add authoritative metadata in the established order; validate the enriched output. | Taking identity/time assertions from generated text or silently substituting missing fields. |
| Accepted-output replay | Compact validated results, including new uncertainty/fields needed by later reasoning; consume the established accepted event/output boundary. | Failed JSON, validation errors, repair instructions, full prompts or raw provider responses. |
| Downstream consumers | Read the final validated contract; update rendering/aggregation/export and replay consumers only where the delta affects them. | Inferring occurrence time from an evidence timestamp or converting uncertainty into a positive finding. |
| Logical prompt identity/version/hash | Update the project's registered logical identity/version and hash of the actual model-visible text when that contract exists; verify request metadata matches. | Inventing versioning where none exists, deriving identity from filenames, or leaving stale metadata after model-visible changes. |

Keep generation prompts focused on behavior, wire hints on exact shapes/examples,
and replay summaries on compact validated results. Edit only the affected surfaces
and synchronize their consumers. Preserve authority, uncertainty, redaction,
application-owned fields and accepted-output-only replay where applicable.

## Map authoritative metadata, not universal field names

Use the [project mapping](resources/project-profile.md) to identify canonical
source IDs, issuance, receipt, processing and occurrence times. They are different
contracts; never substitute a convenient timestamp or generated identity. Missing
required metadata is a controlled failure under the actual contract, not permission
for a model guess. Keep ownership out of model-facing generation/wire examples.
Inject synthetic application metadata before testing the final strict model only
where the mapped final-output boundary requires it.

Preserve the target's actual null rules, accepted-event selection, enrichment and
reconciliation order, stable resource filenames and logical prompt version/hash.
Do not impose a historical schema, vendor field, journal width, retry count or
quote-matching algorithm. Accepted output can include explicitly unverified evidence
only if the actual contract allows it; acceptance is not adjudicated interpretation.

## Verify and deliver

Add deterministic contract/example regression coverage where supported, respecting
the selected lifecycle's testing stage. Structural validity and generation quality
are different claims; model-backed checks require approved tooling/data/protocol.

Check accepted examples and rejection paths: extra/coerced fields, ambiguous or
unknown evidence references, missing authoritative metadata, forged model-owned
timestamps, and failed/repair-only attempts. Confirm that only accepted outputs
reach replay and downstream consumers, and that metadata reflects every changed
model-visible surface. Preserve the application's existing ordering and safety
boundaries rather than adopting an illustrative fixture as production architecture.

Return coordinated authorized edits, rationale, actual regression evidence and
remaining generation uncertainty. In review-only requests make no edits. Source
`prompt` is recorded in the bundled provenance resources. Read
[the coordinated reference and fictional worked case](prompt-worked.md) when
the mapping or acceptance boundary needs a concrete implementation. The case is
self-contained and uses locally supplied fixture inputs without model calls.

develop/backlog.md.content:
Evaluator instruction context.

# Requirement and work-item coverage

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Use this mode for “reconcile these requirements against our tickets and code” or
“identify coverage and ownership gaps.” It produces a coverage register, not a
completion certificate, implementation task, or permission to change a tracker.

Establish authoritative requirements/use cases, decision dates, superseded/conflicting
decisions, declared scope and current work-item metadata. Exhaust relevant pagination
or label incomplete coverage. Absence from one repository is not absence elsewhere.

## Resolve authority and inspection scope

Record source ID/version/date/locator, which claims it governs, and its disposition:
current, superseded, historical proposal, or unresolved conflict. Newer text is not
automatically authoritative for every field. Definitions may come from an approved
specification, exact priorities from an inventory, and execution state from tracker
and implementation evidence. Retain superseded rows in the authority ledger without
double-counting requirements. A portfolio inclusion decision need not authorize
implementation inside an excluded product boundary; carry that conflict to its
owner, while reconciling unblocked requirements normally.

Record tracker query scope and pagination independently of code inspection. Include
relevant parent/child work and terminal/cancelled states; a filtered board is not
the entire backlog. Complete means the selected query's terminal page was reached
and all returned rows were inspected, not that all organizations were searched.
For saved sources distinguish “complete in supplied snapshot” from a fresh live
read. If a cursor/page/source is unavailable, record inspected pages/counts and
missing scope. Then classify an unseen delivery owner as unknown, not a proven
gap. In a complete declared inventory, “no adequate owner in this scope” is a gap,
still not proof of absence in an uninspected tracker or repository.

Map primary delivery, supporting/enabling work and validation separately. Distinguish
implemented baseline, requested increment, partial coverage, ownership gap and
unknown state. A broad use-case reference or related code is not completion.
Refine an appropriate existing owner before proposing duplicate work. Preserve
portfolio priorities without inventing tracker mappings.

## Build the register

Use one row per distinct requirement, with linked work-item roles and explicit
milestones when mixed priorities/scope warrant them. Include:

- Requirement ID/title, authoritative source/version/locator, exact source priority
  and current scope/conflict disposition.
- Implemented baseline and its code/test/artifact evidence; requested increment
  and which observable acceptance criteria are implemented, partial or unevidenced.
- Primary delivery owner; supporting/enabling items; validation owner/evidence.
  Preserve actual work-item type, status, parent and tracker priority separately.
- Dependencies/access/owner decisions; inspection completeness and unknowns;
  bounded existing-owner refinement or a clearly unfiled proposal where needed.

Do not force one item per requirement or call a shared engine the primary delivery
owner of every use case it enables. Done engineering foundations, sandbox proofs,
review sessions, production delivery and approved validation are separate claims.
Keep completed baseline history intact when new feedback asks for an increment.
An In Progress item can lack inspected implementation evidence; a To Do validation
item can have session evidence without an approved completion decision. Record
both rather than silently changing state.

Retain source priority values exactly, including fractional ranks such as `0.5`
and `1.5`, with their source meaning. Tracker `High`, `Unassigned`, roadmap labels,
effort and execution state are different fields. Never map a source rank into an
option, estimate, deadline or state without an approved mapping. Dependency work
may execute first without inheriting its consumer's priority.

Deliver a traceable register of requirement, source/version, owner, implementation
evidence, coverage/status, dependencies and unresolved decisions. Keep this report
separate from Iterate's CLI-owned feature backlog; no automatic state synchronization.
Default read-only. Authorized tracker edits use current metadata, preserve unrelated
values, exhaust necessary pagination and verify read-back. Do not collect sources
or construct research cohorts as a side effect. Historical proposals, even a later
note saying they were filed, grant no mutation authority and do not identify new
live keys without their verified mapping. Ask for an unavailable approved source
only if it blocks the requested conclusion; otherwise report the limitation.

Read [the complete reference and fictional register](backlog-worked.md) for a
concrete multi-source example and deterministic coverage boundary. Source `backlog`
is recorded in the bundled provenance resources. Report actual checks, remaining
unknowns and proposed follow-ups without claiming live refresh or model adherence.

develop/validate-repo.md.content:
Evaluator instruction context.

# Repository validation

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Execute the target project's required checks, inspect affected contracts, preserve
unrelated work, and report local readiness. Select this mode for “Validate these
changes,” “Run the repository checks,” or “Check whether this patch is locally
ready,” as well as `/develop validate-repo [scope]`.

Validation is not authorization for implementation, unrelated fixes, installation,
commits, live LLM evals, or deployment. It must not start a feature lifecycle or
create feature state. Findings do not grant permission to fix them; formatting
and other command effects need the permission check below.

## Establish the state and authority

- Identify the target repository, starting revision, intended changes and allowed
  actions. Read its current instructions, command configuration and affected
  contracts; a historical profile or attached document is context, not consent.
- Before running checks, record staged and unstaged diffs separately, index state,
  and relevant untracked files, including generated/sensitive paths. Record file
  identities or hashes without reproducing secrets. `git status --short`,
  `git diff`, `git diff --cached`, and `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`
  are useful observations, not sufficient proof that mixed edits survived.
- Distinguish intended and unrelated edits even within one file. Note concurrent
  agents' ownership and changes; do not claim an unexplained concurrent mutation
  was caused by a check. Keep a before-state sufficient to compare file content
  and staging without resetting the worktree or creating a commit.
- Map the existing suitable local runtime and prerequisites. An unavailable tool
  or interpreter is environmental, not proof of a broken patch. A missing declared
  production dependency can instead be a contract defect; establish that from
  the project sources, not from an import/setup failure alone.

## Map affected contracts to observations

For each affected area record:

**obligation → authoritative project source → relevant check → observed result**.

Name the current source/section and actual test or command, its tested state and
result. Protect observable behavior and stable documented contracts, not noncontractual
implementation structure or noncontractual event ordering. A label such as
“storage checked” is not evidence. Missing authority, absent behavioral coverage,
or an unperformed check remains a disclosed gap, not a pass. Unaffected areas may
be marked out of scope with a reason.

Use the [generic project mapping](resources/project-profile.md) to record the
target's obligations, language, existing runtime, checks and allowed effects.
The [skills profile](resources/profiles/skills.md) maps this repository only.

## Resolve command effects before execution

Inspect each mapped command's underlying hooks, task/session definitions and
scripts, including invoked commands. Identify formatting/fixes, dependency or
hook installation, network/live calls, generated outputs, cleanup and writes
outside the requested area. Prefer the suitable existing environment, but its
existence does not prove a workflow will not install more dependencies.

Compare **all effects** with permitted scope before execution:

- If covered, run the project's required canonical workflow and record that
  authorization, command, working directory, runtime and affected paths.
- If not covered, explain the specific conflict and request authorization, or
  propose an approved isolated run. Until resolved, the full check is blocked.
  A project instruction requiring a command does not itself authorize every
  side effect of that command.
- An isolated run must contain the intended tested state, including permitted
  dirty/untracked inputs, use the same required checks and a suitable equivalent
  environment, and avoid modifying the original files/index. Obtain permission
  for its remaining installs, network access or cleanup. A clean HEAD-only copy
  cannot validate an uncommitted patch. Do not silently create Git worktrees,
  stash edits, copy sensitive data or treat isolation as permission to install.

A canonical workflow may format/fix files, install dependencies, generate
coverage, clean build outputs or invoke external systems. Hook installation is
separate setup, not validation. A check-only alternative can still have effects;
inspect the actual configuration rather than assuming its name makes it read-only.

Focused tests assist diagnosis; they do not replace required full validation.
Do not silently substitute weaker checks, skip hooks, reduce coverage gates or
claim readiness from focused green tests while the canonical workflow failed or
was omitted. Record the exact command's exit status and meaningful output rather
than inferring success from a summary or an intermediate session.

## Compare and classify

After checks, compare files, staged content and relevant untracked paths with the
recorded before-state. Identify automatic changes separately from requested edits.
Preserve unrelated work, including mixed edits and staged/unstaged separation.
Never automatically reset, delete or unstage changes, including suspicious
artifacts or sensitive configuration; report their paths without secret values
and request a scoped remedy when needed. If preservation cannot be established,
stop and disclose the uncertainty rather than attempting a broad rollback.

Classify each failure using evidence:

| Classification | Required basis |
|---|---|
| Patch-related | Affected behavior/contract evidence or an equivalent baseline pass and tested-patch failure. |
| Baseline-confirmed pre-existing | The same failure reproduced on an identified baseline without the intended patch, using the same command and suitable equivalent inputs/environment; retain both results. |
| Environmental | An observed prerequisite, permissions or environment failure prevents the relevant check. |
| Unresolved | Attribution is not established, including an unavailable baseline or ambiguous concurrent changes. |

An unrelated-looking failure is not automatically pre-existing. Baseline work must
also obey permissions and preserve the original worktree/index. Do not remove
the patch in place to prove attribution. Pre-existing failures remain failed
checks; report “patch not implicated by this evidence,” not “all checks passed.”

Associate every result with the revision plus dirty/untracked inputs actually
tested. Formatter output, fixes and later edits invalidate affected earlier
results; repeat affected checks and the required final canonical workflow when
its inputs changed. Do not repeat unaffected checks merely to generate evidence.

## Report local readiness

Return the scope and tested state; commands, exit statuses and results; contract
mapping/findings; automatic changes; before/after preservation outcomes; failure
classification and supporting baseline evidence; blockers and omitted checks.
Distinguish passed checks from unresolved readiness. All required checks and
affected obligations must have current evidence before an unqualified local-ready
claim; staged sensitive configuration or excluded artifacts is still a finding
even when tests pass.

Local validation never implies live-agent, live LLM eval, deployed-job or
deployed-workload verification. Do not fix findings or enter a feature lifecycle
without a new applicable request. Use the project's existing check engine, not a
duplicate production validation script.

develop/iterate.md.content:
Evaluator instruction context.


# Iterate

For a justified specialization/handoff, read only the relevant [optional recipe](resources/combinations.md).
It does not restart this lifecycle, require sibling installs or replace user checkpoints.

This is the canonical feature lifecycle selected by `/develop iterate`.
Its helper is `scripts/manifest.py` in this skill directory. Parse the parent
mode before resolving work/status/defer/list, contextual targets, or legacy forms
with [shared usage](resources/usage.md#iterate). Read shared policy without silently
changing the lifecycle or state ownership.

Feedback-driven implementation uses persistent project state. Agree direction,
implement a minimal primary flow, exercise it manually, and refine it with the user
before stabilizing the regression suite. Required project checks and essential
access, integrity, and resource protections apply from the start. Only discretionary
completeness is deferred; it is not forgotten or mistaken for safe delivery.

## State Manifest & CLI

State lives in the project repo at `.ai-state/<feature-name>.json`. This file is the source of truth across sessions — always trust it over memory of prior conversations.

The state directory and manifest files must be real local paths, not symlinks. If existing state uses symlinks, stop and explain the policy; do not replace links or move their targets automatically. The user can copy the state into a local `.ai-state/` directory before resuming.

**All manifest reads and writes go through the CLI** bundled as `scripts/manifest.py` in this skill directory. Resolve its absolute path from the installed skill directory, then run `python3 "<skill-directory>/scripts/manifest.py"` from the project root. In the examples below, `manifest.py` means that command; do not assume it is on PATH. Never hand-edit the JSON — the CLI checks required top-level keys, phases, and backlog item fields, stamps `last_updated`, and fails loudly on corruption. Run `manifest.py --help` and `manifest.py <cmd> --help` for full usage.

On damaged state, stop and preserve the file. Ask the user to restore a known-good
local copy or authorize separate maintenance; do not reset, synthesize missing
keys, or interpret validation failure as a missing feature.

The helper validates required nested fields, list entries, actual booleans, and
JSON-compatible values before any handler writes state or updates timestamps.
Duplicate keys, malformed sections, and invalid entry types fail without rewriting
the file. Compatible extra fields and optional `next_step`, `phase_history`, and
`test_bed_commands` omissions remain supported; read-only commands do not backfill
them on disk. Validation does not add phase-order or minimum-option gates.

Tool-registry storage must remain ordinary local directories and a file at
`testbed/tools/registry.json`; links or escaping storage are rejected before access.
Explicitly selected existing external tool references remain supported, but
registration grants no permission to execute them or write an external registry.

| Action | Command |
|---|---|
| New feature | `manifest.py init <feature> --impact "one sentence"` |
| Status dashboard | `manifest.py status [feature] [-v]` (no feature = most recent) |
| List all features | `manifest.py list` |
| Change phase | `manifest.py phase <feature> TWEAKING` (records git commit in `phase_history`) |
| Session handoff note | `manifest.py set <feature> next_step "where things stand"` |
| Render architecture doc | `manifest.py render <feature> [--out PATH]` |
| Park edge case / hardening | `manifest.py park <feature> edge\|hardening "description"` |
| Resolve / waive backlog item | `manifest.py resolve <feature> edge\|hardening <n> [--waive "reason"]` |
| Record test bed command | `manifest.py testbed <feature> add --label "seed db" --cmd "..."` |
| Register / list reusable test bed tools | `manifest.py tool add --name ... --path ... --desc ... [--usage ...] [--feature ...]` / `tool list` |
| Record architecture decision | `manifest.py decision <feature> --title ... --context ... --option A --option B --decision A --rationale ...` |
| Set fields (impact, data_flow, entry_point, exclusion, assertion, ...) | `manifest.py set <feature> <field> "value"` |

## Resolve the requested action

[Shared usage](resources/usage.md#iterate) is the grammar/default authority. These
are assistant instructions, not new helper subcommands.

- Help, bare Iterate, status, and list are read-only. Explain/view the selected
  feature and recency basis when used; no state note, initialization, ignore edit,
  demonstration, or implementation follows. No state means no tracked work.
- Defer and legacy park require an explicit or one human-established feature,
  never modification-time selection. Call the helper with its explicit positional
  ID/kind/description, show the recorded follow-up, and stop. No test/ticket/fix.
- Work and unambiguous legacy feature forms need a resolved target and outcome.
  Show the ID/effect. Resume existing state; a missing resume target is not a new
  feature. Initialize only established start-new intent, ID, and impact; then add
  the local state ignore rule and start ARCHITECTURE. Do not interpret corruption
  or a misspelling as absence. Clarify action-like IDs rather than renaming them.
- An explicit work phase override applies only to the selected existing feature.
  Record the old/new stage, then display status. A new feature begins in architecture;
  a phase record is not proof that earlier exit criteria passed.

Only authorized work adopts the phase constraints. Show its status dashboard and
[readable stage label](resources/usage.md#phases), with real limits and prior
acceptance. Record meaningful work decisions and transitions immediately via the
CLI. Do not write state merely to answer help/status or an argument question.

Manifest schema (managed by the CLI; shown for reference):

```json
{
  "project_metadata": {
    "feature_name": "",
    "last_updated": "",
    "current_phase": "ARCHITECTURE | HAPPY_PATH | TEST_BED | TWEAKING | TESTING | FINALIZATION",
    "next_step": "free-text handoff: exactly where work stands and what happens next",
    "phase_history": [ { "from": "", "to": "", "at": "", "commit": "git sha, if in a repo" } ]
  },
  "core_objective": {
    "impact_target": "one sentence: the exact business outcome this feature delivers",
    "strict_scope_exclusions": []
  },
  "architecture_decisions": [
    { "id": 1, "title": "", "context": "", "options_considered": [], "decision_made": "", "rationale": "" }
  ],
  "implementation_state": {
    "data_flow_description": "inputs -> transformations -> outputs, plus access patterns",
    "test_bed_environment": "prose notes on the environment, if commands alone aren't enough",
    "test_bed_commands": [ { "label": "start services", "command": "docker compose up -d" } ],
    "happy_path_entry_points": []
  },
  "deferred_backlog": {
    "edge_cases": [ { "description": "", "is_resolved": false } ],
    "hardening_tasks": [ { "description": "", "is_resolved": false } ]
  },
  "testing_strategy": {
    "target_execution_path": "",
    "required_integration_assertions": []
  }
}
```

## Universal Rules (all phases)

- **Git permissions are separate.** Phase rituals do not authorize commits,
  branches, squashing, pushes or PR creation. When those actions are not authorized,
  retain the local phase/check summary and user checkpoints without mutating Git.

- **Defer optional completeness.** Record out-of-scope refinements against the
  explicit feature and show the helper's recorded line. Essential safety and in-scope
  correctness are not optional polish: preserve them or contain/block unsafe exercise.
  Do not defer required validation or failure handling merely because of the phase.
- **Phase transitions are explicit.** Obtain required exit agreement before
  advancing, state the next direction, then update via the CLI. Do not imply that
  the helper verifies manual acceptance or ordinary exit criteria.
- **The user can jump phases.** An explicit work `--phase` or unambiguous legacy
  feature/phase request records the selected existing stage. Keep skipped prerequisites
  and unperformed checks visible; do not silently switch implementation approaches.
- **Leave a handoff note.** At the end of every work stint — and before any risky long-running step — run `manifest.py set <feature> next_step "..."` describing exactly where things stand and what happens next (e.g. "handler written, not yet run against docker; seed script at scripts/seed.sh"). The next session's dashboard leads with it; a stale or missing note costs the first ten minutes of that session.

## Comments, Docs & Commits

**Comments:** Write comments only when they add information the code cannot readily convey, such as intent, constraints, or a non-obvious tradeoff. Default to one line; use more when needed for clarity. Keep the voice plain, concrete, and directed at another developer. An available code-commenting skill may help, but none is required.

**Exception — test bed code** (`testbed/` — driver scripts, UI pages, tools) is heavily commented, because the user reads and hand-edits it. The one-line default does not apply there; the same plain voice does. Comments are working notes from one developer to another: what each block does, which lines to change to try different things, gotchas ("server must be up first", "IDs must exist in the seed data"). Keep it casual and concrete — `# bump this to see pagination kick in`, not `# This variable controls the number of rows fetched per request`. No section-banner ASCII art, no docstring boilerplate, nothing that reads like generated documentation.

**Commits** — the git history must read as if a developer wrote it, with no trace of the AI workflow:

**Local-only projects:** If the project has no Git repository, or the user explicitly chooses a local-only trial, record that choice as an architecture decision using the CLI and mention it in `next_step`. Proceed through the same six phases with the same user checkpoints. Do not initialize Git or create a remote merely to satisfy this skill. Omit commits, squashing, pushes, and PRs in local-only mode; record phase transitions without a commit SHA and summarize the local changes and checks instead. A Git project without a usable remote can use this mode after the user chooses it. FINALIZATION then starts after the local TESTING exit and resolves each item after its focused check, without waiting for a nonexistent PR merge.

- **Commit only at the end of a phase** that produced code (typically HAPPY_PATH, TWEAKING, TESTING, FINALIZATION; skip phases that changed nothing tracked). Commit first, then run `manifest.py phase` — the recorded SHA then anchors exactly what that phase produced. No mid-phase WIP commits unless the user asks.
- **Never commit specs or planning artifacts:** `.ai-state/`, plan/design docs, and feature-specific test bed scratch (`testbed/scratch/`); gitignore both at init. **Exception — reusable test bed tools:** pieces likely useful to future features (seed scripts, UI shells, server wrappers) are promoted to `testbed/tools/`, registered via `manifest.py tool add`, and committed along with `registry.json` — they are temporary tooling, kept generic (no feature-specific hardcoding). Do the promotion at TWEAKING or FINALIZATION exit, when it's clear which pieces earned reuse; when in doubt whether something is reusable, ask the user. If a test bed artifact is worth keeping (a seed script others would use), that's a deliberate decision to surface to the user, not a default.
- **Commit messages:** imperative subject line under ~65 chars stating what changed; body only when it earns it — the why, a constraint, or a tradeoff the diff can't show, in one or two short paragraphs of plain prose. No bullet-list inventories of the diff, no phase names or workflow vocabulary ("happy path", "parked", "FINALIZATION"), no co-author/generated-by trailers.

**Product-facing documentation** should describe the product, not irrelevant
delivery-process detail. Skill/workflow manuals must define their inputs, effects,
checkpoints, and limits; architecture/progress reports may show state and phases.
All prose should read like a developer writing for a colleague:

- **Plain words over jargon.** Write for someone who knows the language but not this system. If a term is load-bearing, define it once in a sentence and then use it; if it's decoration, cut it.
- **No flourish.** No "seamlessly", "robust", "powerful", "leverage", "elegant", "under the hood", "it's worth noting that", "in today's fast-paced". No selling the feature — the reader already decided to use it. No exclamation marks.
- **Say the thing, then stop.** One idea per paragraph, two to four sentences. No paragraph that restates the previous paragraph in different words, no closing summary that repeats the page.
- **Concrete over abstract.** A short runnable example beats three paragraphs describing what the example would show. Real identifiers and realistic data, not `foo`/`bar`.
- **Lead with the sharp edges.** The things that actually cost someone an afternoon — the failure that looks like a bug but is a config error, the call that must happen first, the default that surprises — get their own headings or callouts. That's what makes a doc worth reading over the source.
- **No AI tells.** No emoji, no bold-lead bullet lists where every bullet is `**Word** — sentence`, no rhetorical questions as headings, no "Let's dive in", no tables of one-word cells padded to look thorough.
- **Keep the topic clear.** Omit internal process jargon from unrelated product
  docs. When the workflow itself is the topic, explain load-bearing terms rather
  than suppressing phases, state, or follow-up information.

```text
# Wrong (reads like an AI wrote it):
Bentobox's powerful access control system seamlessly empowers you to
secure your artifacts! Under the hood, it leverages a flexible
attribute-based paradigm. Let's dive into how it works.

# Right:
Artifacts can carry an access policy. Once one does, every Hub method
that touches it asks whether the current caller is allowed.

Bentobox does not authenticate anyone and does not store attributes
about anyone. Your application knows who the caller is, and answers
the question when asked.
```

Document settled product behavior alongside its tests and accepted flow. Usage,
safety, and workflow-contract changes need accurate guidance when they change;
they do not wait for a feature phase. Use existing docs navigation and applicable
render checks under their permissions; do not invent a new docs site.

**Pull requests — the goal is a small, reviewable main PR:**

- **The main PR is the happy path plus its tests, and nothing else.** It ships at TESTING exit, before any backlog work. Squash the phase commits into one, push the branch, and open the PR. Everything the workflow deferred stays deferred — that's what keeps the diff small enough for a human to actually read.
- **Each FINALIZATION item is its own follow-up PR** — one edge case (or one closely-related pair), its fix, and its reproducing test, branched off the merged main PR. A reviewer who has already accepted the happy path can review a fifteen-line hardening diff in a minute.
- The PR description is the commit message with a line on how to exercise the feature. Same discipline: no phase names, no workflow vocabulary, no bullet inventory of the diff.
- **The main PR closes with a "Follow-ups" list** — the open backlog, one line per item, plus waived items marked as such with their reason. This is what tells a reviewer the thin diff is deliberate: they can see the malformed-input case and the duplicate-call case are known and coming, rather than assuming they were missed. Generate it from `manifest.py status <feature> -v`, but write it as plain prose lines a reviewer understands out of context ("Rejects duplicate webhook deliveries", not "edge_cases[2]"). Each follow-up PR references the main PR and drops its item from the remaining list.

```text
# Wrong (reads like an AI wrote it):
Implement HAPPY_PATH for csv-import feature

- Added POST /api/csv-import endpoint
- Parses CSV with header row and inserts rows
- Edge cases parked for FINALIZATION phase

# Right:
Add CSV import endpoint feeding the dashboard table

Rows go straight into the table the dashboard already reads,
so no new query path. Assumes a header row; malformed and
oversized files are rejected upstream by the ALB body limit.
```

## Phases

### 1. ARCHITECTURE
Decide direction before code. For each major decision (data storage, access pattern, new service vs. module, sync vs. async, etc.):
- Compare genuine options for unsettled material choices. Reuse an adequate
  approved specification/discussion and verify current assumptions instead of
  manufacturing another options exercise; actual user direction agreement remains.
- Record the outcome in `architecture_decisions` (context, options, decision, rationale).
- Define `data_flow_description`: inputs, outputs, access patterns.
- Write the one-sentence `impact_target` and list `strict_scope_exclusions` (things explicitly NOT in v1).
- **Plan the test bed:** run `manifest.py tool list` and inventory what exists. Identify which registered tools this feature can reuse as-is, which need modification, and which new tools it will need — record the outcome in `test_bed_env` (e.g. "reuse seed-db and ui-shell; extend seed-db with a row-count knob; new: webhook-catcher"). TEST_BED then executes this plan instead of discovering it.

No implementation code in this phase. **Exit when:** major decisions are recorded and the user agrees on direction.

**On exit, ask the user** if they want the architecture doc generated: `manifest.py render <feature> --out <path>` produces a markdown summary (objective, scope, data flow, decisions, test bed plan) from the manifest. It's a generated artifact — regenerate rather than edit it, and never commit it.

### 2. HAPPY_PATH
Implement the primary outcome with its required contracts and protections.
- Defer speculative extensions, optional resilience, and unrelated polish. Do not
  ban required validation, failure handling, or authorization to preserve phase purity.
- Existing project checks and necessary safety-contract verification may occur early.
  Stabilize the wider regression suite after feedback; code-before-test is not BDD.
- Record entry points in `happy_path_entry_points`.

**Exit when:** the primary flow is code-complete against the recorded data flow,
with essential protections checked or the exercise safely contained. Full manual
acceptance follows demonstration/refinement; do not certify unchecked behavior.

### 3. TEST_BED
Make the primary flow manually exercisable through the smallest architecture-agreed
surface: existing application UI, CLI/sample files, native driver/REPL, or a thin page.
Require both web and Python only if acceptance genuinely needs both. The helper's
Python runtime requirement does not dictate the demo language. The test bed is a
feature playground, not a skill dashboard, production interface, automated test
suite, or model-evaluation pipeline.

Keep representative permitted inputs, visible end-to-end outputs/side effects,
editable variables, and reproduction commands. A new server, notebook, dependency,
restricted data source, or live model call needs its actual project/user permission;
no demonstration rule supplies it. No generic scaffolding for planning or checks.

Execute the existing tool plan rather than discovering it again. Feature-local
scratch stays in `testbed/scratch/<feature>`; reuse approved tools before creating
new ones. Shared-tool changes remain generic and preserve old defaults; otherwise
keep a feature-local copy. Update registry usage when an authorized shared invocation
changes; promotion to reusable tooling is deliberate, not an automatic side effect.

Record each successful startup/seed/exercise command with its label through the
helper. Reusing a label replaces it while preserving ordering; remove obsolete
labels explicitly. Run the actual primary flow once and report the result, including
failure, before handing the agreed mechanism to the user. Preserve their edits.

**Exit when:** the agreed mechanism works as a reproducible way to exercise the flow,
an end-to-end observation is recorded, and the user can try it. A reproducible flow
failure can enter refinement; it is not a passed acceptance check.

### 4. TWEAKING
Tight loop: change → run against test bed → observe → repeat. This loop is shared with the user — they try the agreed task-appropriate surface and edit its representative inputs; expect their edits and feedback to drive changes.
- Keep changes small and observable; verify each by re-running the recorded commands (`manifest.py testbed <feature> list`), not by reading code.
- Keep the agreed demonstration working as the feature changes — it is the verification surface for the whole loop. Before touching a user-editable demo, read its current contents immediately before editing and apply a targeted patch that preserves user changes. Scratch files are ignored by Git, so do not rely on `git diff` to detect their edits; do not regenerate the driver wholesale.
- Park only explicitly optional future improvements; required correctness, validation and safety remain in scope.
- Log any decision reversals in `architecture_decisions` (new entry, don't rewrite history).

**Exit when:** the user says the behavior feels right.

### 5. TESTING
Few tests, each one earning its keep.
- Prefer **one comprehensive integration test per flow** that exercises the same path validated in the test bed, over many mocked unit tests. Set `target_execution_path` to that flow.
- Each test should assert the things that would actually break: outputs, side effects, persisted state — list them in `required_integration_assertions` first, then write the test to cover them.
- Protect accepted behavior and required safety contracts; optional deferred
  cases wait for their agreed item. Earlier essential checks do not become
  test-first evidence, and existing green behavior is not manufactured red.

**Exit when:** the happy-path tests pass and run green from a clean environment. In Git/PR mode, ship the main PR: squash the feature branch's commits into one, push, and open it (see Pull requests above). Confirm with the user before pushing. In local-only mode, record the local delivery summary and checks instead. The backlog does not block this; it follows after.

### 6. FINALIZATION
Consume the backlog and interrogate the result. In Git/PR mode, the main PR may still be open: wait for it to merge before creating finalization branches, then branch each item from the updated target branch containing that merge. In local-only mode, start after the local TESTING exit and use the focused-check delivery rule above instead of branches and PRs.
- Work through the backlog **one item at a time** (`manifest.py status <feature> -v` lists them with indexes). No batching — finish and `resolve` one before starting the next.
- **Before touching code for each item, present a short briefing** and pause for the user's take if they're present:
  1. **Why it exists** — the mechanism: what input, state, or timing produces this case, and how likely it is in practice.
  2. **Impact if unhandled** — what actually goes wrong (corrupt data, crash, silent wrong answer) and who hits it.
  3. **Proposed prevention** — the fix in a couple of sentences, at the level of approach not diff.
  4. **Tradeoffs** — what the fix costs (complexity, performance, UX friction, new dependencies) and any alternative worth naming, including "waive it" when the case is unlikely and the fix is expensive.
- Then implement it **with an explicit test that reproduces the edge case** — the test triggers the exact condition from the briefing (the malformed input, the duplicate call, the mid-operation failure) and asserts the prevented outcome. One focused test per edge case, on its own branch off the main PR, opened as its own PR; only then `resolve`. Waived items (`resolve ... --waive "reason"`) get no code and no test. Never leave an item silently unaddressed.
- **After resolving each item, stop and ask the user before starting the next one.** Summarize what was done in a sentence, name the next item, and wait for their go-ahead — this is a hard checkpoint, not a courtesy; do not continue on an unanswered question or assume consent from earlier enthusiasm. The backlog survives in the manifest, so stopping mid-list loses nothing.
- Run the hardening checklist against the final code and park findings as `hardening` items:
  null/empty/malformed inputs · authn/authz on new surfaces · secrets not logged or committed · timeouts and resource cleanup on external calls · concurrent/duplicate invocation · failure mid-operation (partial writes) · pagination or size limits on unbounded data.
- Finish with a short summary: what shipped, what was deliberately excluded, any backlog items left open.

**Exit when:** backlog is fully resolved-or-waived and checklist findings are addressed.

## Red Flags — you are drifting

| Thought | Correction |
|---|---|
| "I'll add unrelated resilience while I'm here" | Defer optional scope; required safety/failure contracts cannot wait. |
| "Every check must wait until TESTING" | Required project/safety checks can occur early; stabilize the wider suite after manual feedback. |
| "This abstraction will help later" | Later hasn't been validated. Write the concrete version. |
| "I remember where we left off" | The manifest is the truth. Read it. |
| "I'll update the manifest at the end" | Sessions die. Update after each step. |
| "Let me commit this progress" mid-phase | Commits land at phase boundaries only. |
| "I'll fold the edge cases in before opening the PR" | The main PR is the happy path. Edge cases are follow-up PRs. |
| "The intro paragraph should sell the feature" | Docs are jargon-free and unflowery. State what it does, then stop. |
| "The plan doc should go in the repo" | Planning artifacts stay local. The code and its commit message are the record. |

Evaluator instruction context.

# Code review

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Review whether the declared change or current implementation is desirable,
well-placed, correct and maintainable. This is a source-grounded review, not an
automatic repository-wide audit or permission to apply the recommendations.

For a complete ordered review and consolidated revised review, selectively load
[the worked review](code-worked.md). Its supplied snapshots support every location;
its illustrative report is not an observed model evaluation.

Use this mode to decide whether the declared implementation/change is acceptable.
When the requested outcome is instead a structural inventory and remediation
plan for a subsystem, select `smells`; a source sample does not establish a whole
repository review. General code explanations need neither assessment mode.

## Establish the review contract

- Identify the target and actual snapshot: supplied diff/PR and established base,
  or explicitly selected current-source scope. Account for workspace edits when
  those are the target. Without a base, do not claim a defect was introduced by
  an unknown change.
- Read current project instructions, the PRD or other requirements, relevant
  architectural direction and protected contracts. Trace changed code through its
  callers, tests, documentation and configuration as needed to assess consequences;
  distinguish supporting inspection from expanding the finding scope.
- Load available prior findings when re-reviewing. Establish which earlier scope
  and snapshot they described; do not invent a previous review when none is supplied.
- Establish existing users, public consumers and compatibility requirements.
  A historical prompt's pre-user assumption is not evidence about this project.
  If cleanroom/pre-user status is established, apply the cleanup policy below;
  otherwise preserve known contracts and label consequential unknowns.
- Separate failures caused only by the review environment from code defects.
  Missing `pyarrow` or another hard dependency in an atypical environment is not
  itself a finding. An undeclared required production dependency can be a finding
  when supported by packaging and runtime evidence. Disclose checks that could
  not run; continue independent source inspection without pretending they passed.

## Review in this order

1. **Intent:** Does the change solve the right problem? Is the feature, behavior
   or cleanup desirable under the requirements and likely use cases? Identify
   unnecessary or misdirected work before polishing its implementation.
2. **Architecture:** Is responsibility in the right place? Does the design fit the
   current project structure and intended direction, with sensible dependencies,
   APIs and module boundaries?
3. **Implementation:** Is behavior correct, maintainable and reasonably simple?
   Are tests proportionate and meaningful, documentation accurate, and the PRD,
   implementation, tests and docs consistent with one another?
4. **Polish:** Inspect naming, wording, consistency and important nits that improve
   clarity, maintainability or contributor onboarding. Do not let nits displace a
   more consequential intent or design issue.

## Coverage checklist

Use these as inspection lenses, not a finding quota. Substantiate claims with
actual use and a concrete consequence.

| Lens | What to establish |
|---|---|
| Dead, unused or underused code | Callers, registration, supported extension points and whether the remaining benefit justifies the surface. Low usage alone is not proof of dead code. |
| Generalization, specialization and overengineering | Whether abstractions, layers, options or one-off special cases serve real requirements rather than hypothetical users or obsolete designs. |
| Leaky abstractions | Whether callers must know implementation details or repair a boundary's incomplete contract. |
| Risky duplication | Repeated algorithms, schema knowledge, configuration or policies that can diverge; distinguish matching behavior from merely similar syntax. |
| Unnecessary complexity | Branching, modes, mutable state and indirection that make behavior or changes harder to reason about. |
| Documentation complexity | Overly verbose, duplicated or complicated docs that obscure the usable contract or increase synchronization work; retain necessary explanations. |
| Test design | Fragile, inconsistent or overengineered tests, implementation coupling, redundant setup and missing behavioral coverage. |
| Cross-file consistency | Conflicting coding standards or architectural approaches; assess the project's actual conventions rather than personal taste. |
| Layout and ownership | Whether directories, modules and responsibility boundaries are logical, discoverable and easy to follow. |
| Historical names and surfaces | Names, APIs, module boundaries and file organization reflecting former designs instead of today's intended design. |
| Contract alignment | Inconsistencies among the PRD, implementation, tests, docs and configuration, including missing or contradictory acceptance behavior. |
| Removal opportunities | Unnecessary code, tests, docs, configuration, compatibility branches, old references or dead paths; use the established compatibility policy. |
| Reviewability | Changes too large, broad or mixed-purpose to assess effectively. Name the separable concerns and recommend a coherent split; disclose what remains unreviewed. |

Do not spend findings on formatting, routine lint or other issues correctly handled
by automation. Inspect the automation when the diff shows it is missing,
misconfigured or inconsistently applied; report that underlying gap instead of
enumerating every mechanically detectable symptom.

## Choose a decisive, complete remedy

Consider the reasonable solution space, then recommend **one preferred solution**
for each important issue. Balance correctness, simplicity, maintainability,
project consistency and likely users/use cases. The smallest textual patch is
not the objective: prefer the cleanest, clearest, lowest-complexity design that
fully addresses the cause, including relevant tests/docs/configuration.

Make the handoff sufficiently prescriptive for a junior developer: identify what
to remove or move, which boundary should own behavior, what contracts remain,
and how to verify the outcome. Avoid "consider refactoring" without a concrete
direction. Offer alternatives only for a real unresolved tradeoff the available
context cannot settle; explain the decision-changing evidence rather than
leaving an open-ended menu.

When cleanroom/pre-user status and no compatibility obligations are established:

- Do not preserve legacy behavior, old references, dead paths, defensive
  compatibility layers, deprecated APIs or migration mechanisms solely for
  hypothetical existing users. Recommend removing obsolete surfaces rather than
  adding another compatibility wrapper.
- Prefer fixing worthwhile nits and optional cleanup now, especially clarity,
  consistency, maintainability and onboarding improvements. Deferral needs a
  concrete reason such as disproportionate effort or a genuinely separate concern.
- State whether this assumption changes each recommendation. No existing users
  does not erase current behavioral, security, data or architectural requirements.

Outside cleanroom, honor actual consumers and migration obligations. Unknown
compatibility is not removal permission. "Fix now" describes the recommendation,
not authorization for the reviewer to edit code or widen the task.

## Finding contract

Each actionable finding includes:

1. A stable ID, short title, verified file/line location and the actual evidence.
2. **Urgency** and **feedback type**, using the separate scales below.
3. The issue and why it matters: concrete behavioral, maintenance or contributor
   consequence, not a broad stylistic assertion.
4. One preferred complete fix and why it balances simplicity and completeness;
   identify relevant contracts and behavioral validation.
5. Whether it is worth fixing now, with the reason for any deferral.
6. Compatibility assumptions and whether established no-users/no-compatibility
   status changes the fix or its timing.
7. Introduced, worsened or relevant pre-existing status when a real comparison
   supports it; otherwise say introduction is unknown.

| Urgency | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Must fix before merging | A merge blocker supported by the requirements or consequences. |
| Should fix now | Important correction or cleanup that should accompany the change. |
| Optional, but recommended now | Non-blocking improvement worth doing in this revision; default for worthwhile cleanroom nits. |
| Optional, can defer | A justified separate or lower-value improvement; give the reason. |

| Feedback type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| TODO | Must be addressed before merge. |
| Question | Needs an answer, but may not require code changes. |
| Follow-up | Worth considering separately; explain why separation is appropriate. |
| Nit | Small improvement with a clarity, consistency or maintainability benefit. |

Keep urgency separate from impact severity and the structural audit's S0–S3 scale.
Use compatible labels: do not call a deferrable item a mandatory TODO. A question
is for a consequential unknown, not a substitute for making a supported decision.

## Re-review and delivery

Return a consolidated review, not just an appended list of new findings. Recheck
prior claims against current raw evidence: update still-open items, resolve
verified fixes, withdraw stale/unsupported claims with reasons, and merge duplicates
while retaining their IDs as aliases. Add new findings without losing earlier
in-scope concerns. Mark prior items outside the revised scope as not reassessed;
do not silently drop them or call them fixed.

Use the requested output format, including valid JSON when requested, and rank
actionable findings by consequence and urgency. Include scope/snapshot, comparison
limits, reviewed and unreviewed areas, and actual checks with passed/failed/not-run
or blocked status. Do not claim full coverage from a sample. No actionable findings
is a valid result. Do not edit files or post the review without separate authority.

# Consequence-grounded structural audit

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Audit the declared source for structures that make change, testing, security or
operations materially harder. Inspect actual contracts and consequences; size
alone is not a finding. The [current coverage map](source-coverage.md) records the
maintained diagnostic mechanisms and their evidence requirements.

Load [the worked audit](smells-worked.md) when a complete evidence-to-remedy example
would help: divergent terminal policy, event ownership, scattered configuration,
useful no-findings and incomplete coverage. Its fictional inputs define the task's
contracts and accessible scope.

Use this mode when the requested outcome is structural diagnosis and a maintenance
plan for a declared scope. Assessing whether a particular implementation/change
is acceptable belongs to `code`. A generic question about smells is an explanation,
not authorization to inspect a repository or refactor its code.

## Scope and inventory

- Declare subsystem/repository boundaries, current workspace or commit snapshot,
  language, architecture, public invariants and compatibility requirements.
  Inspect relevant callers, tests and configuration to understand the target.
- For the report-equivalent Python scope, inventory **all production and
  repository-support Python files**, including relevant hidden support directories
  such as CI scripts. Exclude tests, virtual/generated environments and
  non-production experiments from the finding scope unless the user requests them.
  They may still provide supporting evidence; label that distinction. Honor an
  explicitly different scope or language rather than forcing Python defaults.
- Track every eligible file as reviewed, partially reviewed or unreviewed. Calculate
  file/line counts from the actual snapshot if reporting them, explain the counting
  basis, and separate inventory totals from inspected totals. Never reuse the
  any historical file counts, metrics or source locations.
- Inventory responsibility and mutable-state clusters, collaborators, repeated
  algorithms and schema knowledge, and changes requiring coordinated edits. Trace
  actual uses before judging the design; a missing source limits the claim.

## Evidence threshold and counterexamples

A finding needs an identifiable maintenance, change-locality, testability,
security or operational consequence. Explain which change becomes scattered,
which state or policy can diverge, which boundary leaks, or which invariant is at
risk. Size and branch counts can support the explanation but do not prove it.

Do not label DTOs, protocols, package markers, boundary adapters or cohesive long
routines solely because of their size or shape. Check whether a data object names
a real contract, a protocol has useful consumers, a facade preserves a purposeful
public boundary, or a wrapper adds validation/normalization rather than mere
forwarding. Declarative constants and table-driven step definitions can centralize
variation rather than create a smell. Broad catches at CLI/command/logging
boundaries can be proportionate exception translation; inspect their effect, not
just their syntax. Likewise, a lengthy lookup or budget algorithm may be cohesive.

Separate a supported design consequence from a preference and from a direct
correctness defect. State counterevidence and uncertain runtime consequences;
do not elevate "could diverge" to a demonstrated failure without evidence.

## Diagnostic families and concrete probes

Use these diagnostic families where actual consequences support them. Apply those
relevant to the declared scope; there is no requirement to find all ten or introduce
the named design patterns everywhere.

| Family / diagnostic pattern | Inspect and substantiate | Preferred direction when supported |
|---|---|---|
| Bloaters / Large Class; Divergent Change; Couplers / Solution Sprawl (F01) | Unrelated responsibility clusters such as orchestration, retry, tool execution, persistence, failure translation and result construction sharing broad mutable state or collaborators. Show independent reasons to change and focused-test costs. | Keep a purposeful public facade, extracting cohesive collaborators at actual ownership seams rather than splitting by line count. |
| Dispensables / Duplicated Code; Object-Orientation Abusers / Combinatorial Explosion (F02) | Repeated state machines with differing counters, terminal behavior, repairs or validation. Compare transitions and genuinely different completion policies, not just similar loops. | Extract one shared transition loop with a narrow policy/callback and small distinct completion handlers; avoid multiplying boolean modes. |
| Bloaters / Long Parameter List and Data Clumps; Duplicated Code (F03) | Primitive run/step/error/event fields repeatedly forwarded through helpers and serializers, especially a failure path that bypasses the normal recorder. Trace defaults, redaction, indexing and persistence ownership. | Introduce a cohesive event draft/context value and one recorder for index assignment, serialization and persistence; retain the required storage schema at the boundary. |
| Change Preventers / Shotgun Surgery; Long Method (F04) | One setting duplicated across allowed keys, typed settings, precedence, coercion, validation, deployment env names, render arguments and templates. Enumerate the coordinated-edit sites. | Own field/default/env/coercion metadata once and consume it in runtime/deployment paths; separate scalar parsing from cross-field invariants. |
| Bloaters / Long Method, Long Parameter List and Data Clumps (F05) | A packaging routine mixing acquisition, normalization, token estimates, repeated whole-context reconstruction, truncation search, parallel mutable accumulators, metrics and payload presentation. Identify the coupled stages and identity/budget fields. | Use a cohesive request/context value, a budget allocator returning blocks/outcomes, and a separate public payload presenter. Do not fragment a cohesive budget algorithm solely because it is long. |
| Long Method; Object-Orientation Abusers / Conditional Complexity (F06) | A reconciliation pipeline mixing dynamic-shape parsing, source lookup, fuzzy correction, mutation, final-attempt policy, status counters and diagnostics. Trace branches updating the same accumulators. | Parse typed candidates, reconcile each to a result, then reduce results into payload/metadata; make differing mismatch policy explicit rather than a threaded boolean. |
| Divergent Change; Long Method (F07) | Graph construction, nested closures, parse-state history, validation, repair prompts, evidence reconciliation and safe/final result projection sharing a module. Check whether temporary state is per-run or closure-held. | Retain the registry-facing factory where it is a contract; separate validation/reconciliation and projection, with explicit per-run validation context. |
| Conditional Complexity; Couplers / Inappropriate Intimacy (F08) | Orchestration branching on internal tool dictionaries while also owning transitions, retry guidance, templates, events and evidence-source presentation. Look for guards reconstructing argument shapes independently. | Adapt raw tool content once into stable outcome values, isolate the acquisition transition policy, and keep presentation outside it. |
| Dispensables / Oddball Solution and Duplicated Code (F09) | Multiple row adapters using mappings, indexing or `asDict()` with inconsistent copying, required fields and exception contracts. Verify that their domain requirements actually match. | Own one validated row adaptation contract at the storage/provider boundary; let domain mappers consume it without leaking provider-specific shape knowledge. |
| Object-Orientation Abusers / Conditional Complexity (F10) | An expanding assertion catalog requiring fields, validation, branching, result changes and CLI rendering, particularly domain rules mixed with generic checks. | Use typed assertion specifications and a small evaluator registry only when it consolidates real variation; keep domain-specific assertions separate from generic path/equality/list checks. |

One finding may span several families. Name the actual smell and consequence,
not every possible catalog label. These source patterns are not a complete Python
smell guide or exclusive list of problems the current source may exhibit.

## Remedy design and preserved behavior

Recommend one preferred remedy that lowers total complexity and change risk,
not merely the smallest patch or the greatest number of extractions. Typed
values, registries, adapters and state machines must centralize ownership or make
a contract clearer, rather than relocate the same branches behind indirection.
Avoid hypothetical extension mechanisms and additional boolean mode combinations.

Identify the behavior the remedy must preserve: transition and event ordering,
retry/terminal rules, errors and diagnostics, redaction, serialization defaults,
indexes, append-only schemas, configuration precedence/coercion, budget outcomes,
safe outputs, public APIs and security boundaries, as relevant. Preserve known
consumers and compatibility; establish cleanroom only from current target evidence. If
the current task establishes cleanroom, obsolete compatibility surfaces can be
removed, but present behavioral/data/security requirements still apply.

State the behavioral validation needed for those invariants and whether it already
exists, was run or remains proposed. Pure structural changes can use existing
characterization tests; do not manufacture a failing test to justify a refactor.
The audit does not itself authorize tests with external effects or implementation.

## Findings and severity

Each finding includes a stable ID and title, S-level, family/specific smell,
verified current file/line locations, structural evidence, concrete consequence,
one preferred remedy with rationale, protected invariants and needed validation.
When using metrics, derive them from the inspected source. Do not copy historical
IDs, metrics, locations or severity judgments as newly verified findings.

| Structural severity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| S3 | Correctness or operational risk. |
| S2 | Significant design risk. |
| S1 | Maintainability concern. |
| S0 | Observation; distinguish it from actionable defects. |

Keep S0–S3 separate from merge urgency, feedback type and Debate impact labels.
Do not infer one scale from another. Rank findings by supported consequence;
no minimum count or severity distribution is required.

## Report and remediation order

Deliver the requested format; the report-equivalent default includes:

1. **Scope and method:** snapshot, inclusions/exclusions, actual inventory/inspection
   counts when available, evidence sources and missing guide or source limitations.
2. **Executive summary:** useful existing boundaries and the principal structural
   pressure points, not a generic verdict or a claim that everything needs rewriting.
3. **Ranked findings:** the evidence/remedy contract above, with multiple verified
   locations when the consequence crosses files.
4. **File-by-file coverage ledger:** every in-scope file maps to finding IDs,
   "No material finding", partial review or unreviewed with a reason. "No material
   finding" means inspected structure is proportionate to its role, not perfection;
   it cannot describe an unread file. Note useful counterexamples where relevant.
5. **Dependency-aware remediation:** explain which seam reduces risk for later
   changes, then order independent and smaller work. For example, one event
   draft/recorder can precede runner-loop extraction; configuration centralization
   can proceed independently; typed item/acquisition pipelines and smaller row/
   assertion consolidation follow where their dependencies justify it. This is
   a planning example, not a prescribed sequence for every project.
6. **Checks and limits:** actual versus proposed/unperformed validation and
   incomplete inspections. No findings is a valid bounded result.

For a revised audit, reassess prior findings against the new snapshot and retain
their dispositions/IDs without duplicating or silently dropping concerns. Keep
the audit read-only; proposed remediation does not authorize a refactor or posting.

# Current method coverage and public design boundaries

This map describes the maintained methods, diagnostic mechanisms and verification
scope. The [public design ledger](resources/provenance.json) records current
contracts and qualified public attribution. Actual findings require the selected
target's source and authority; inventory and semantic inspection are separate.

## Implementation assessment

[Code review](code.md) retains Intent -> Architecture -> Implementation -> Polish;
all checklist families; automation-gap exceptions; one complete supported remedy;
actual consumers and conditional cleanroom cleanup; urgency/type/timing distinctions;
and consolidated open/resolved/withdrawn/aliased/not-reassessed prior claims.
[The fictional worked review](code-worked.md) exercises identity, ambiguity, consumer
compatibility and source-grounded revised dispositions through its supplied inputs.

## Ten structural diagnostic mechanisms

Every mechanism is explicit in [structural audit](smells.md), not limited to the
three example findings in [the fictional worked audit](smells-worked.md).

| Mechanism | Evidence and preferred boundary |
|---|---|
| Multiple reasons to change / solution sprawl | Cohesive collaborators behind a purposeful facade. |
| Duplicate transition loops / combinatorial explosion | One loop with narrow policy, not more boolean modes. |
| Primitive event clumps / recorder bypass | Typed context and one index/serialization/persistence owner. |
| Distributed configuration / shotgun surgery | Shared field metadata; scalar parsing versus cross-field invariants. |
| Multi-stage budget packaging | Request context, allocator outcomes and payload presentation. |
| Mixed parsing/correction/mutation/final-attempt policy | Typed candidates, per-item results and explicit mismatch policy. |
| Factory/closure/validation/projection entanglement | Dedicated validation/projection and per-run context. |
| Raw tool dictionaries crossing acquisition/guards/presentation | Stable outcomes and separate transition/presentation boundaries. |
| Divergent row adapters | One provider-boundary adapter only where contracts actually match. |
| Mixed domain/generic assertion catalogs | Typed specs and a small registry only when ownership becomes simpler. |

Keep the consequence threshold, S0-S3 independent of urgency/impact, useful DTOs,
protocols, facades, boundary catches and cohesive long routines. Every selected
file is inspected, partial or unreviewed explicitly. Remediation ordering follows
actual dependencies, not a copied refactoring sequence or fixed defect count.

## Intentional generalizations and limits

The generic project mapping resolves actual identities, time, permissions,
configuration, diagnostics, domain decisions, readiness, provisioning and recovery.
Map the target's schema, scope and acceptance from its authoritative instructions.
Examples define only their own contracts. Missing required evidence blocks the
relevant conclusion; generated accounts or similarities cannot supply it.

Behavioral red/green fixture checks and package integrity are local observations,
not agent adherence, host routing, scientific validity or recovered upstream fidelity.
Keep all candidate IDs and unresolved source/authority disputes through explicitly
selected Debate. Consensus is not evidence and missing stages are incomplete.

# Technical discussion

For inputs, context/defaults, named controls and effects, use
[the shared usage reference](resources/usage.md).

Establish the decision, current baseline, authoritative constraints, relevant raw
artifacts, alternatives and consequential unknowns. Compare genuine options using
correctness, simplicity, ownership, compatibility, likely use and operational cost.
Prefer one supported decision; expose genuine unresolved business/access/domain
tradeoffs rather than force consensus or a menu of unsupported fixes.

Separate verified source claims, conditional hypotheses and preferences. Inspect
counterevidence and consequential omissions; disagreement is not a defect. Honor
requested output format and explain evidence/limits. Discussion is read-only and
does not authorize implementation, model calls or publication by itself.

Single-pass is default. Explicit `--engine debate` uses the existing bundled
hierarchy and its model/host preflight without changing scope or permissions.
